Thank you for submitting your article "Proteasome storage granules protect proteasomes from autophagic degradation upon carbon starvation." for consideration by eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by Jonathan Cooper (Senior Editor) and three reviewers, one of whom, Raymond J Deshaies (Reviewer #1), is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

This paper proposes a role for proteasome storage granules (PSGs) in protecting proteasomes from autophagy. PSGs form when yeast cells are starved of carbon source. They are rapidly dissolved upon re-feeding. Interestingly, PSGs do not form upon nitrogen starvation, and instead the proteasomes are taken up into the vacuole by autophagy (which the authors refer to as proteaphagy) and degraded. A key observation in the paper is that in cells doubly starved for carbon and nitrogen, proteasomes enter in to PSGs and are not subject to proteaphagy. Furthermore, mutations (e.g. ∆blm10) that prevent PSG formation upon carbon starvation result in proteophagy. By contrast, treatments that promote PSG formation (e.g. 2-deoxyglucose) block proteophagy upon nitrogen starvation. The authors go on to show that there is a strong correlation between PSG formation and speed of growth recovery upon re-feeding starved cells. This suggests that an important function of PSGs is to allow cells to preserve their proteasomes in times of carbon starvation stress, such that they can quickly recover when more resources are available.

Essential revisions:

A key finding of this work is that formation of PSGs correlates with more rapid recovery from starvation. Most of the data on this point are correlative, and it is difficult to rule out that the treatments used do not exert their effect through perturbing or promoting some process other than PSG formation. With this in mind, there are two experiments that would strengthen this key section of the paper that the reviewers believe should be done:

1) Repeat the ∆ubp3 rescue experiment with a mutant other than ∆blm10 (e.g. ∆nat3; a ∆nat3 ∆ubp3strain should recover from carbon starvation faster than ∆nat3), to establish that this effect is not limited to one particular mutant/treatment.

2) Examine the effect of ∆ubp3 on recovery from starvation in ∆spg5. This is a key experiment because proteaphagy in carbon-starved ∆spg5 is not blocked by introducing ∆ubp3. Thus, a ∆spg5 ∆ubp3 strain should not show more rapid resumption of growth compared to ∆spg5, in the assay shown in Figure 8K. This would be particularly striking because ∆ubp3 does have a beneficial effect when this assay is performed with ∆blm10, and thus would greatly strengthen the correlation between low proteaphagy and rapid resumption of growth.

In addition, given that this paper shows for the first time the behavior of PSGs in Arabidopsis, the authors should evaluate whether these structures are reversible as they are in yeast.

Reviewer #1:

The authors have examined the ability of cells of different genotype or treated with different agents to recover upon re-feeding following nitrogen, carbon, or nitrogen and carbon starvation. These experiments paint a consistent picture: if a cell can form PSGs upon starvation to protect its proteasomes from proteophagy, it recovers more rapidly upon refeeding. My one comment here is that I would like to see the ∆ubp3 rescue in more than one example. Currently, the authors show that ∆ubp3 will rescue the recovery defect of a ∆blm10 mutant. Is that same true for ∆nat3, for example?

The other major concern I have is that it is hard to exclude that PSGs form for some other reason other than to protect the proteasome from proteophagy. The authors could address this by being a bit more circumspect in their Discussion. The recovery experiments described in the prior paragraph provide further support for this contention, but given that all of the mutants analyzed are likely to impact multiple physiological processes, it is difficult to exclude that the major protective effect of Blm10 or Nat3 is through some process other than PSG formation.

Another issue that is not addressed is why formation of PSGs would protect from autophagy? There is a paragraph in the Discussion devoted to this topic but it focuses almost entirely on how/why PSGs form and says little about how formation of these structures would prevent autophagy. Autophagy can clearly process large structures including mitochondria and IPODs. Why would formation of PSGs be protective? Perhaps the authors can include a few lines on this in the Discussion.

Reviewer #2:

In the present study, the authors show that the formation of proteasome storage granules (PSGs), which are formed under carbon-starvation conditions, antagonizes proteaphagy. The CP and RP are separated when the ATP level is reduced, but both accumulate at the same PSGs. They further show that autophagic degradation of proteasomes, which is inhibited by the PSG formation, delays the resumption of cell growth after carbon starvation-replenishment, suggesting a reservoir function of PSGs. Finally, the authors show this phenomenon also in Arabidopsis.

Overall, this study is well performed and presented. The methods used in this study are appropriate. Remaining questions would be how PSGs are able to escape from autophagic degradation and how de-ubiquitination is important for proteaphagy. However, these could be future studies as the authors have made significant progress in revealing a role of PSG formation in protection from autophagic degradation and cell regrowth after starvation.

Reviewer #3:

Marshall and Vierstra report that PSGs and proteaphagy function antagonistically in regulating proteasome abundance during carbon and nitrogen starvation in both yeast and plant cells. PSGs help protect proteasomes from autophagic degradation upon carbon starvation, and promote cell fitness upon recovery from carbon starvation. In carbon-starved cells, the sequestration of the proteasome core particle (CP) into PSGs is dependent on Blm10, while the deposition of the regulatory particle (RP) into PSGs is facilitated by Spg5. In the absence of Blm10, which redirects CPs to the vacuole, active Ubp3 is required for CP proteaphagy under carbon starvation. Assembly of PSG-like structures and protection of proteasomes from proteaphagy under fixed carbon starvation can be reproduced in Arabidopsis. Whether these PSG-like structures in Arabidopsis can be rapidly remobilized upon recovery from carbon starvation is unknown.

Overall, this manuscript provides important biological insight into at least one function of PSG formation. The idea that PSGs act to protect functional proteasomes from autophagy under carbon starvation, or energy-depleted, conditions (and possibly the same for other cellular 'puncta') is attractive and well supported by the data. The paper is also well written and well organized. I think the paper would be suitable for publication in eLife after the modest criticisms, suggestions, and corrections below are addressed:

o The apparent mass of the cleaved GFP in the western blots from yeast extracts (Ex. Figures 1A-1C) was larger than what would be expected. In contrast, the free GFP MW from plant protein extracts was close to the expected size (Figures 9A, 10A). Please explain this difference.

o Can the cytoplasmic foci (Figure 1D) be rapidly remobilized to the nucleus after switching to fresh YPGA that has 2% glycerol? Similarly, can the 2-DG-induced cytoplasmic foci (Figure 3E) remobilize upon switching to fresh +N +C medium?

o What percentage of cells have separate cytoplasmic foci of Pre10-GFP and Rnq1-mCherry in Figure 1H?

o As shown in Figure 5F, some mCherry-Spg5 puncta colocalize with Rpn5-GFP in carbon-starved cells, which seems inconsistent with the description in the last paragraph of the subsection “Spg5 helps deliver the RP to PSGs and protects the RP from proteaphagy”. Similarly, some mCherry-Spg5 puncta colocalized with Pre10-GFP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C); again this is inconsistent with the description in the text. Please address this apparent discrepancy, and more importantly, provide the percentage of PSGs marked by Rpn5 or Pre10 that co-localize or not with Spg5.

o In Figure 7C, what is the GFP cleavage profile for Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP in the ∆ubp3 mutant?

o For the starvation treatments on 5-day-old Arabidopsis seedlings, is there data indicating the nutrients from seeds are exhausted at this time point? Also, ConA was only added to the medium for starvation treatments. Could ConA cause proteasome relocalization to form cytoplasmic foci in Arabidopsis even when grow in nutrient rich medium?

o In Figure 9, can these PSG-like structures in Arabidopsis be remobilized into nuclei upon carbon restoration? It would be nice, but not essential, in establishing the parallels with yeast PSGs, to show whether these PSG-like structures in Arabidopsis roots behave similarly compared to the PSGs in yeast.

o There is no description of the methods used for plant protein extraction as far as I can tell.

o I did not see any details or citation for the atg7-2 mutant line used in Figure 10D.

claims.evidence: This is supported by data showing that deletion of Blm10 blocks CP entry into PSGs and deletion of Spg5 delays RP entry into PSGs, along with co-localization studies.

claims.claim: Modulating PSG formation by perturbing cellular energy status or pH influences the rate of proteasome degradation.
claims.source: Modulating PSG formation, either by perturbing cellular energy status or pH, or by genetically eliminating factors required for granule assembly, not only influences the rate of proteasome degradation, but also impacts cell viability upon recovery from carbon starvation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experiments using 2-DG to deplete ATP and by growing cells at different pH levels, showing inverse relationships between PSG formation and proteaphagy.

claims.claim: Modulating PSG formation by genetically eliminating factors required for granule assembly influences the rate of proteasome degradation.
claims.source: Modulating PSG formation, either by perturbing cellular energy status or pH, or by genetically eliminating factors required for granule assembly, not only influences the rate of proteasome degradation, but also impacts cell viability upon recovery from carbon starvation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experiments with mutants lacking Blm10, Nat3, Mdm20, Spg5, and Rpn11 variants, showing that blocking PSG formation accelerates proteaphagy.

claims.claim: Modulating PSG formation impacts cell viability upon recovery from carbon starvation.
claims.source: Modulating PSG formation, either by perturbing cellular energy status or pH, or by genetically eliminating factors required for granule assembly, not only influences the rate of proteasome degradation, but also impacts cell viability upon recovery from carbon starvation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by growth resumption assays showing that mutants unable to form PSGs have delayed growth recovery after carbon starvation.

claims.claim: PSG formation and concomitant protection against proteaphagy also occurs in Arabidopsis.
claims.source: PSG formation and concomitant protection against proteaphagy also occurs in Arabidopsis, suggesting that PSGs represent an evolutionarily conserved cache of proteasomes that can be rapidly re-mobilized based on energy availability.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experiments in Arabidopsis showing PSG-like structures upon fixed-carbon starvation and accelerated proteaphagy in pa200 mutants.

claims.claim: PSGs represent an evolutionarily conserved cache of proteasomes that can be rapidly re-mobilized based on energy availability.
claims.source: PSG formation and concomitant protection against proteaphagy also occurs in Arabidopsis, suggesting that PSGs represent an evolutionarily conserved cache of proteasomes that can be rapidly re-mobilized based on energy availability.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PSGs form in both yeast and Arabidopsis and that they rapidly dissociate upon return to nutrient-rich conditions.

claims.claim: Proteasomes undergo rapid proteaphagy in response to nitrogen starvation in yeast.
claims.source: While yeast proteasomes undergo rapid proteaphagy in response to nitrogen starvation (Marshall et al., 2016), recent results from Waite et al., 2016 suggested that proteasomes are not similarly degraded in response to carbon starvation, even though both conditions activate bulk autophagy (Takeshige et al., 1992; Adachi et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by prior published work and confirmed by GFP-release assays in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Proteasomes are not similarly degraded in response to carbon starvation compared to nitrogen starvation, even though both conditions activate bulk autophagy.
claims.source: While yeast proteasomes undergo rapid proteaphagy in response to nitrogen starvation (Marshall et al., 2016), recent results from Waite et al., 2016 suggested that proteasomes are not similarly degraded in response to carbon starvation, even though both conditions activate bulk autophagy (Takeshige et al., 1992; Adachi et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and confirmed by GFP-release assays and Pho8Δ60 activity assays in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Greater than 90% of both Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP fusions disappeared within 1 day of the onset of nitrogen starvation.
claims.source: Greater than 90% of both fusions disappeared within 1 day of the onset of starvation, concomitant with the strong accumulation of free GFP.
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the GFP-release assay data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Loss of Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP fusions and the release of free GFP were substantially slower upon carbon starvation compared to nitrogen starvation.
claims.source: By contrast, loss of the fusions and the release of free GFP were substantially slower upon carbon starvation, which was generated by switching cells from growth on non-fermentable carbon (i.e. glycerol) to medium lacking this carbon source (Takeshige et al., 1992; Adachi et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the GFP-release assay data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Free GFP was undetectable within the first 2 days of carbon starvation, with only small amounts appearing subsequently (~8–12% after 6 days).
claims.source: Here, free GFP was undetectable within the first 2 days, with only small amounts appearing subsequently (~8–12% after 6 days; Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the GFP-release assay data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The carbon starvation regime employed effectively suppressed culture growth.
claims.source: This relative absence of proteaphagy occurred despite that fact that the carbon starvation regime employed here effectively suppressed culture growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and stimulated bulk autophagy, as judged by the increased activity of the Pho8Δ60 reporter (Noda and Klionsky, 2008) and by the release of free GFP from GFP-Atg8, which both measure autophagic flux (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the growth curve data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The carbon starvation regime employed stimulated bulk autophagy, as judged by the increased activity of the Pho8Δ60 reporter and by the release of free GFP from GFP-Atg8.
claims.source: This relative absence of proteaphagy occurred despite that fact that the carbon starvation regime employed here effectively suppressed culture growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and stimulated bulk autophagy, as judged by the increased activity of the Pho8Δ60 reporter (Noda and Klionsky, 2008) and by the release of free GFP from GFP-Atg8, which both measure autophagic flux (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the Pho8Δ60 activity assay and GFP-Atg8 release assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: The modest accumulation of free GFP from the Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP reporters upon carbon starvation was autophagy-dependent.
claims.source: This modest accumulation of free GFP seen from the Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP reporters was autophagy-dependent, as it was absent in mutants eliminating the core autophagy component Atg7, or the Atg13 regulatory subunit of the Atg1 kinase complex that activates autophagy in response to nutrient deprivation (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the GFP-release assay data in Δatg7 and Δatg13 mutants shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Proteaphagy still occurs in yeast upon carbon starvation, but at a substantially slower rate than upon nitrogen starvation.
claims.source: Thus, proteaphagy still occurs in yeast upon carbon starvation, but at a substantially slower rate.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the GFP-release assay data showing slow accumulation of free GFP upon carbon starvation.

claims.claim: Rapid proteaphagy during nitrogen starvation was suppressed by the simultaneous lack of carbon.
claims.source: Surprisingly, when nitrogen and carbon starvation were combined, we found that rapid proteaphagy during nitrogen starvation was suppressed by the simultaneous lack of carbon.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the GFP-release assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Although 8 hr of nitrogen starvation induced rapid clearance of proteasomes, little to no clearance was evident in cells starved for both nitrogen and carbon.
claims.source: Although 8 hr of nitrogen starvation induced rapid clearance of proteasomes, as measured by loss of the Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP reporters together with the appearance of free GFP, little to no clearance was evident in cells starved for both nitrogen and carbon (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the GFP-release assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The turnover of GFP-tagged substrates related to the CVT pathway, pexophagy, ribophagy, and mitophagy is induced by nitrogen, carbon, or simultaneous nitrogen and carbon starvation.
claims.source: This contrasted with other forms of selective autophagy, with the turnover of GFP-tagged substrates related to the cytoplasm-to-vacuole targeting (CVT) pathway (Ape1; Shintani et al., 2002), pexophagy (Pex14; Reggiori et al., 2005), ribophagy (Rpl25; Kraft et al., 2008) and, to a lesser extent, mitophagy (Om45; Kanki and Klionsky, 2008) being induced by all three starvation regimes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the GFP-release assay data for various selective autophagy substrates shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Carbon starvation selectively suppresses proteaphagy, despite up-regulating both bulk autophagy and other forms of selective autophagy.
claims.source: Taken together, it appears that carbon starvation selectively suppresses proteaphagy, despite up-regulating both bulk autophagy and other forms of selective autophagy.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing that carbon starvation induces bulk autophagy and other selective autophagy pathways but not proteaphagy.

claims.claim: Upon switching exponentially growing cells from nitrogen-rich to nitrogen-starvation medium, the GFP signals from Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP moved from a mainly nuclear localization to a diffuse vacuolar pattern within 24 hr.
claims.source: Upon switching exponentially growing cells from nitrogen-rich to nitrogen-starvation medium, the GFP signals moved from a mainly nuclear localization to a diffuse vacuolar pattern within 24 hr (Figure 1E and F).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claims.claim: The relocation of Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP to the vacuole upon nitrogen starvation was not evident in cells starved for both nitrogen and carbon.
claims.source: Strikingly, this relocation was not evident in cells starved for both nitrogen and carbon.
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claims.claim: Upon simultaneous nitrogen and carbon starvation, the Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP signals migrated toward the nuclear periphery and into brightly fluorescent, large (~0.5 μm) puncta within the cytoplasm.
claims.source: Instead, the Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP signals migrated toward the nuclear periphery and into brightly fluorescent, large (~0.5 μm) puncta within the cytoplasm (Figure 1E and F).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claims.claim: The appearance of cytoplasmic puncta containing Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP was extremely rapid, being detectable in 50% of the cells within 1 hr of carbon starvation and in 95% of the cells after 4 hr.
claims.source: The appearance of these foci was extremely rapid, being detectable in 50% of the cells within 1 hr of carbon starvation and in 95% of the cells after 4 hr (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claims.claim: The time course for entry of Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP into cytoplasmic puncta (within 1 hr) was faster than the up-regulation of bulk autophagy (at 2 to 4 hr).
claims.source: The time course for entry of Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP into these cytoplasmic puncta (i.e. within 1 hr) was faster than the up-regulation of bulk autophagy (at 2 to 4 hr), suggesting that formation of these foci is an early response to carbon deprivation separate from autophagy.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparing the time course of PSG formation with the time course of bulk autophagy induction.

claims.claim: The cytoplasmic puncta containing Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP were visible in mutants missing Atg1, Atg11, Atg13 and Atg17, indicating that they arise independent of autophagy.
claims.source: In support, the foci were visible in a number of mutants missing factors required for autophagy initiation, including Atg1, Atg11, Atg13 and Atg17 that help scaffold the pre-autophagosomal structure (PAS), indicating that they arise independent of autophagy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data in autophagy mutants shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: The appearance of cytoplasmic puncta containing Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP was rapidly reversible; upon switching starved cells to fresh carbon-containing medium, the GFP signals returned to diffuse cytoplasmic and nuclear patterns within 30 min.
claims.source: The appearance of these foci was also rapidly reversible; upon switching starved PRE10-GFP or RPN5-GFP cells to fresh carbon-containing medium, the GFP signals returned to diffuse cytoplasmic and nuclear patterns within 30 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: The proteasome-containing puncta emerging after carbon starvation were different from IPODs, as co-localization studies with Pre10-GFP and the IPOD marker Rnq1-mCherry detected separate cytoplasmic foci in greater than 90% of cells.
claims.source: However, the proteasome-containing puncta emerging after carbon starvation were different, as co-localization studies with Pre10-GFP and the IPOD marker Rnq1-mCherry (Kaganovich et al., 2008) detected separate cytoplasmic foci in greater than 90% of cells (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the co-localization confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: The rapid accumulation of proteasomes into the cytoplasmic puncta seen upon carbon starvation still occurred in Δhsp42 cells, while the accretion of inactive proteasomes into IPODs requires the Hsp42 chaperone.
claims.source: Moreover, while the accretion of inactive proteasomes into IPODs requires the Hsp42 chaperone (Figure 1G; Marshall et al., 2016), the rapid accumulation of proteasomes into the cytoplasmic puncta seen here upon carbon starvation still occurred in Δhsp42 cells (Figure 1G; Peters et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data in Δhsp42 cells shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: The proteasome-containing foci seen upon carbon starvation are different from IPODs.
claims.source: These data place the proteasome-containing foci seen upon carbon starvation as different from IPODs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization and Hsp42-dependence data.

claims.claim: The cytoplasmic puncta seen upon carbon starvation are PSGs.
claims.source: Numerous studies have described the accumulation of PSGs in stationary phase yeast which resemble the proteasome-containing puncta seen here that form during carbon starvation (Laporte et al., 2008; Peters et al., 2013; Saunier et al., 2013; van Deventer et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2016; Gu et al., 2017; reviewed in Chowdhury and Enenkel, 2015; Yedidi et al., 2016). Consequently, we hypothesized that these puncta are PSGs, which could protect proteasomes from proteaphagic degradation by sequestering them away from the autophagic machinery.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of the observed puncta to previously described PSGs and is supported by subsequent experiments.

claims.claim: PSGs could protect proteasomes from proteaphagic degradation by sequestering them away from the autophagic machinery.
claims.source: Consequently, we hypothesized that these puncta are PSGs, which could protect proteasomes from proteaphagic degradation by sequestering them away from the autophagic machinery.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis that is subsequently tested and supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: The protein acetylase NatB is essential for PSG assembly.
claims.source: One such situation involves the protein acetylase NatB, one of three acetylation complexes in yeast that modify the N-terminus of proteins in a sequence-dependent manner (Polevoda et al., 1999). Genetic analysis of both its catalytic (Nat3) and regulatory (Mdm20) subunits recently demonstrated that NatB is essential for PSG assembly (van Deventer et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by prior published work and confirmed by the data in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Both the Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP reporters failed to localize to PSG-type foci in Δnat3 and Δmdm20 cells subjected to carbon starvation.
claims.source: Here, we confirmed this observation by showing that both the Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP reporters failed to localize to PSG-type foci in Δnat3 and Δmdm20 cells subjected to carbon starvation (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: In Δnat3 and Δmdm20 cells subjected to carbon starvation, both Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP reporters accumulated in the vacuole.
claims.source: Instead, both reporters accumulated in the vacuole, as expected if proteaphagy became the alternative.
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Whereas little free GFP accumulated from both Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP reporters even upon extended carbon starvation of wild-type cells, rapid GFP accumulation was seen in Δnat3 and Δmdm20 cells.
claims.source: Likewise, whereas little free GFP accumulated from both reporters even upon extended carbon starvation of wild-type cells, rapid GFP accumulation was seen in Δnat3 and Δmdm20 cells (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the GFP-release assay data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Both the accumulation of PSGs and the stability of the Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP fusions were restored to wild-type levels when Δnat3 cells were rescued with HA-tagged Nat3, but not with the catalytically defective Nat3(C97A)-HA variant.
claims.source: Both the accumulation of PSGs and the stability of the Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP fusions were restored to wild-type levels when Δnat3 cells were rescued with HA-tagged Nat3, but not with the catalytically defective Nat3(C97A)-HA variant (Figure 2A and B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), demonstrating that an active NatB complex is essential for PSG assembly and proteaphagy suppression.
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy and GFP-release assay data shown in Figure 2A and B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: An active NatB complex is essential for PSG assembly and proteaphagy suppression.
claims.source: Both the accumulation of PSGs and the stability of the Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP fusions were restored to wild-type levels when Δnat3 cells were rescued with HA-tagged Nat3, but not with the catalytically defective Nat3(C97A)-HA variant (Figure 2A and B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), demonstrating that an active NatB complex is essential for PSG assembly and proteaphagy suppression.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the complementation data showing that only catalytically active Nat3 can rescue the phenotype.

claims.claim: The rpn11-m5 mutation blocks entry of the RP into PSGs and encourages transport of the RP to the vacuole in response to carbon starvation.
claims.source: In a similar fashion, we tested a pair of mutants affecting the intrinsic deubiquitylase of the RP, Rpn11 (termed rpn11-m1 and rpn11-m5; for details see Materials and methods), which were previously shown to prevent or delay entry of the RP, but not the CP, into PSGs (Saunier et al., 2013). Accordingly, we found that both the rpn11-m1 and rpn11-m5 alleles suppressed formation of PSGs containing Rpn5-GFP upon carbon starvation, and instead allowed concentration of the reporter in vacuoles (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The rpn11-m1 and rpn11-m5 mutants promoted the rapid release of free GFP from the Rpn5-GFP reporter but not the Pre10-GFP reporter upon carbon starvation.
claims.source: The mutants also promoted the rapid release of free GFP from the Rpn5-GFP reporter but not the Pre10-GFP reporter, indicating that proteaphagy of the RP, but not the CP, was now occurring in these carbon-starved cells (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the GFP-release assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The responses of rpn11-m5 cells were restored to wild type when complemented with an RPN11-FLAG transgene.
claims.source: In both assays, the responses of rpn11-m5 cells were restored to wild type when complemented with an RPN11-FLAG transgene (Figure 2C and D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy and GFP-release assay data shown in Figure 2C and D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Small amounts of free GFP accumulated from the Rpn5-GFP reporter in the rpn11-m1 mutant even in the absence of starvation.
claims.source: Interestingly, small amounts of free GFP accumulated from the Rpn5-GFP reporter in the rpn11-m1 mutant even in the absence of starvation (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the GFP-release assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The slight accumulation of free GFP from Rpn5-GFP in the rpn11-m1 mutant in the absence of starvation was absent in Δatg7 and Δcue5 backgrounds, suggesting that it represents proteaphagy of compromised RPs.
claims.source: This slight accumulation was absent in Δatg7 and Δcue5 backgrounds (data not shown), suggesting that it represents proteaphagy of compromised RPs, as previously observed for the rpn5ΔC mutation that also impairs RP assembly (Peters et al., 2015; Marshall et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the accumulation is autophagy-dependent and is consistent with prior observations.

claims.claim: Growth at low pH accelerates the accumulation of PSGs, while growth in high pH medium dampens their accumulation.
claims.source: In the latter situation, growth at low pH, as occurs during quiescence, accelerates the accumulation of PSGs, while growth in high pH medium dampens their accumulation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by prior published work and confirmed by the data in the manuscript.

claims.claim: PSG accumulation was more robust at low pH and dampened at high pH.
claims.source: While PSG accumulation, as assessed by confocal fluorescence microscopy, was more robust at low pH and dampened at high pH (Figure 3A; Peters et al., 2013), we found that rates of proteaphagy, as measured by release of free GFP from the Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP reporters, were more robust at high pH and dampened at low pH (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Rates of proteaphagy were more robust at high pH and dampened at low pH.
claims.source: While PSG accumulation, as assessed by confocal fluorescence microscopy, was more robust at low pH and dampened at high pH (Figure 3A; Peters et al., 2013), we found that rates of proteaphagy, as measured by release of free GFP from the Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP reporters, were more robust at high pH and dampened at low pH (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the GFP-release assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: High pH encouraged transport of the GFP signals to the vacuole, in agreement with increased proteaphagy.
claims.source: High pH also encouraged transport of the GFP signals to the vacuole, in agreement with increased proteaphagy (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The rapid appearance of free GFP from both Pre10-GFP and Rpn5-GFP reporters in pH 9.0 medium was blocked in Δatg1, Δatg7 and Δatg13 mutants, but allowed in Δcue5 mutants.
claims.source: This rapid appearance of free GFP from both reporters in pH 9.0 medium was blocked in Δatg1, Δatg7 and Δatg13 mutants, but allowed in Δcue5 mutants (Figure 3C), indicating that clearance of proteasomes at high pH occurred via the nutrient-responsive proteaphagy pathway, and not by the pathway that clears inactive proteasomes (Marshall et al., 2016; Waite et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the GFP-release assay data in various mutants shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Clearance of proteasomes at high pH occurred via the nutrient-responsive proteaphagy pathway, and not by the pathway that clears inactive proteasomes.
claims.source: This rapid appearance of free GFP from both reporters in pH 9.0 medium was blocked in Δatg1, Δatg7 and Δatg13 mutants, but allowed in Δcue5 mutants (Figure 3C), indicating that clearance of proteasomes at high pH occurred via the nutrient-responsive proteaphagy pathway, and not by the pathway that clears inactive proteasomes (Marshall et al., 2016; Waite et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential dependence on autophagy components.

claims.claim: Culture growth was robust at pH 6.0, but substantially slower in pH 3.0 or pH 9.0 media.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that culture growth was robust at pH 6.0, but substantially slower in pH 3.0 or pH 9.0 media (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the growth curve data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Changes in the growth medium pH only marginally impacted bulk autophagy, based on measurements of autophagic flux using the Pho8Δ60 reporter.
claims.source: However, changes in the growth medium pH only marginally impacted bulk autophagy, based on measurements of autophagic flux using the Pho8Δ60 reporter (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the Pho8Δ60 activity assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Pre-treatment of non-starved, wild-type cells with 5 mM 2-DG rapidly induced the sequestration of proteasomes into PSG-type puncta.
claims.source: As predicted, pre-treatment of non-starved, wild-type cells with 5 mM 2-DG rapidly induced the sequestration of proteasomes into PSG-type puncta, as observed by confocal fluorescence microscopy (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The PSG-type puncta induced by 2-DG strongly resembled the puncta observed following carbon starvation, including their rapid reversibility when 2-DG was removed from the culture medium.
claims.source: Their appearance strongly resembled the puncta observed following carbon starvation, including their rapid reversibility when 2-DG was removed from the culture medium (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claims.claim: PSGs appeared in nitrogen-starved cells pre-treated with 2-DG, as they do in cells subjected to simultaneous nitrogen and carbon starvation.
claims.source: In fact, PSGs even appeared in nitrogen-starved cells pre-treated with 2-DG, as they do in cells subjected to simultaneous nitrogen and carbon starvation.
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: 2-DG dampened proteaphagy induced by nitrogen starvation.
claims.source: In contrast, when assayed for proteaphagy by the GFP-release assay of both reporters, we found that 2-DG had the inverse effect; like carbon starvation, 2-DG dampened proteaphagy induced by nitrogen starvation (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the GFP-release assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Conditions that suppress PSG formation (the Δnat3, Δmdm20, rpn11-m1 and rpn11-m5 mutations, or growth at high pH) accentuated proteaphagy, while those that enhanced PSG formation (low pH and 2-DG) instead dampened proteaphagy.
claims.source: Taken together, we found that conditions that suppress PSG formation (the Δnat3, Δmdm20, rpn11-m1 and rpn11-m5 mutations, or growth at high pH) accentuated proteaphagy, while those that enhanced PSG formation (low pH and 2-DG) instead dampened proteaphagy, strongly suggesting that the two processes are inversely related.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing inverse relationships between PSG formation and proteaphagy under various conditions.

claims.claim: The two processes (PSG formation and proteaphagy) are inversely related.
claims.source: Taken together, we found that conditions that suppress PSG formation (the Δnat3, Δmdm20, rpn11-m1 and rpn11-m5 mutations, or growth at high pH) accentuated proteaphagy, while those that enhanced PSG formation (low pH and 2-DG) instead dampened proteaphagy, strongly suggesting that the two processes are inversely related.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing inverse relationships between PSG formation and proteaphagy under various conditions.

claims.claim: Blm10 (known as PA200 in plants and mammals) is a well-described CP capping factor.
claims.source: Blm10 (known as PA200 in plants and mammals) is a well-described CP capping factor, where it has been proposed to help assemble α- and β-subunits into the CP barrel, stabilize the complex before RP docking, and/or possibly promote nuclear import of the CP (Schmidt et al., 2005; Sadre-Bazzaz et al., 2010; Dange et al., 2011; Weberruss et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by prior published work.

claims.claim: Blm10 has been implicated in PSG assembly, where it appears essential for sequestering the CP specifically.
claims.source: This 246-kDa protein has also been implicated in PSG assembly, where it appears essential for sequestering the CP specifically (Weberruss et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by prior published work and confirmed by the data in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The Pre10-GFP reporter did not localize into PSGs in Δblm10 cells after 24 hr of carbon starvation, but instead appeared in the vacuole.
claims.source: Indeed, we found by confocal fluorescence microscopy that the Pre10-GFP reporter did not localize into PSGs in Δblm10 cells after 24 hr of carbon starvation, but instead appeared in the vacuole (Figure 4A and B), strongly suggesting an absolute requirement for Blm10 in directing the CP to PSGs.
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: There is an absolute requirement for Blm10 in directing the CP to PSGs.
claims.source: Indeed, we found by confocal fluorescence microscopy that the Pre10-GFP reporter did not localize into PSGs in Δblm10 cells after 24 hr of carbon starvation, but instead appeared in the vacuole (Figure 4A and B), strongly suggesting an absolute requirement for Blm10 in directing the CP to PSGs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the CP fails to enter PSGs in the absence of Blm10.

claims.claim: The Rpn5-GFP reporter behaved normally in carbon-starved Δblm10 cells and rapidly coalesced into PSGs.
claims.source: By contrast, the Rpn5-GFP reporter behaved normally in carbon-starved Δblm10 cells and rapidly coalesced into PSGs (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: The appearance of Pre10-GFP in Δblm10 vacuoles upon carbon starvation was blocked in Δatg7 and Δatg13 backgrounds, but not in the Δcue5 background.
claims.source: The appearance of Pre10-GFP in Δblm10 vacuoles upon carbon starvation was blocked in Δatg7 and Δatg13 backgrounds, where the Pre10-GFP reporter instead remained in the cytosol and nucleus, but not in the Δcue5 background (Figure 4A and B), indicating that autophagic transport of the CP proceeds via the nutrient-responsive proteaphagy pathway, and not the pathway that clears inactive proteasomes.
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Autophagic transport of the CP in Δblm10 cells proceeds via the nutrient-responsive proteaphagy pathway, and not the pathway that clears inactive proteasomes.
claims.source: The appearance of Pre10-GFP in Δblm10 vacuoles upon carbon starvation was blocked in Δatg7 and Δatg13 backgrounds, where the Pre10-GFP reporter instead remained in the cytosol and nucleus, but not in the Δcue5 background (Figure 4A and B), indicating that autophagic transport of the CP proceeds via the nutrient-responsive proteaphagy pathway, and not the pathway that clears inactive proteasomes.

results.result: Proteasomes undergo rapid proteaphagy upon nitrogen starvation but not carbon starvation in yeast. Carbon starvation instead stimulates rapid sequestration of proteasomes into cytoplasmic puncta (PSGs), which form independently of autophagy machinery and are rapidly reversible. Simultaneous nitrogen and carbon starvation suppresses nitrogen starvation-induced proteaphagy.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C30 provide converging evidence from GFP-release assays (C13-C15, C18-C21), confocal microscopy (C24-C27, C29-C30), bulk autophagy measurements (C16-C17), and time-course analyses (C27-C28) demonstrating differential proteasome fates under nitrogen versus carbon starvation. The data consistently show rapid proteaphagy under nitrogen starvation and PSG formation under carbon starvation, with appropriate controls for autophagy dependence.

results.result: The proteasome-containing puncta formed upon carbon starvation are distinct from IPODs and represent PSGs that could protect proteasomes from proteaphagy.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 provide direct experimental evidence through co-localization studies with IPOD markers and Hsp42-dependence experiments showing the puncta are distinct from IPODs. Claims C34-C35 establish the identity as PSGs based on similarity to previously described structures and propose a protective function, which is subsequently tested and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

results.result: The NatB N-terminal acetylation complex (Nat3/Mdm20) is essential for PSG assembly and proteaphagy suppression, requiring catalytic activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C41 demonstrate through confocal microscopy (C37-C38), GFP-release assays (C39), and complementation studies with catalytically active and inactive variants (C40-C41) that NatB is essential for PSG formation and prevents proteaphagy. The requirement for catalytic activity is rigorously demonstrated through rescue experiments with wild-type and mutant Nat3.

results.result: The rpn11-m1 and rpn11-m5 mutations block RP entry into PSGs and promote selective proteaphagy of the RP but not the CP.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 provide confocal microscopy and GFP-release assay data showing that rpn11 mutations selectively affect RP but not CP localization and degradation, with complementation confirming specificity. Claims C45-C46 provide additional mechanistic insight into constitutive RP proteaphagy in rpn11-m1 mutants, supported by autophagy-dependence experiments.

results.result: Intracellular pH inversely regulates PSG formation and proteaphagy: low pH promotes PSG formation and suppresses proteaphagy, while high pH has opposite effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 demonstrate through confocal microscopy (C48, C50) and GFP-release assays (C49, C51) that pH inversely affects PSG formation and proteaphagy, with autophagy-dependence experiments (C51-C52) confirming the pathway. Claims C53-C54 provide important controls showing that pH effects are not simply due to growth inhibition or general autophagy changes.

results.result: ATP depletion by 2-DG treatment induces PSG formation and suppresses proteaphagy, demonstrating an inverse relationship between PSG formation and proteaphagy.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 provide confocal microscopy and GFP-release assay data showing that 2-DG treatment induces PSGs and suppresses proteaphagy, with rapid reversibility upon 2-DG removal. Claims C59-C60 synthesize multiple lines of evidence (NatB, Rpn11, pH, 2-DG) to establish the inverse relationship between PSG formation and proteaphagy.

results.result: Blm10 is essential for CP entry into PSGs and protects the CP (but not RP) from proteaphagy. Blm10 co-localizes with the CP in PSGs and is itself protected from autophagy under PSG-forming conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C70 provide comprehensive evidence through confocal microscopy (C63, C65-C66), GFP-release assays (C68-C70), and autophagy-dependence experiments (C66-C67, C69) demonstrating Blm10's essential role in CP protection. Claims C71-C77 establish through co-localization studies (C71-C74) and GFP-release assays (C75-C76) that Blm10 enters PSGs with the CP and is protected from autophagy, supporting the protective function of PSGs.

results.result: Ecm29 is not required for PSG formation or proteaphagy regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 provide GFP-release assay data showing that Δecm29 cells behave like wild-type for both PSG-mediated protection and nitrogen/inhibitor-induced proteaphagy, ruling out a role for this proteasome-associated protein in the processes under study.

results.result: Spg5 promotes RP entry into PSGs and protects the RP (but not CP) from proteaphagy, though its effect is partial rather than absolute. Unlike Blm10, Spg5 does not consistently co-localize with PSGs and is not detected in purified proteasomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C91 provide confocal microscopy (C83-C85), GFP-release assays (C89-C90), autophagy-dependence experiments (C87-C88), and time-course analyses (C91) demonstrating Spg5's role in RP protection, with the important distinction that the effect is partial (C85-C86). Claims C92-C95 establish through co-localization studies and mass spectrometry that Spg5 does not follow the RP into PSGs, distinguishing its mechanism from Blm10.

results.result: The CP and RP dissociate upon carbon starvation but are sequestered separately into PSGs via distinct pathways. Co-purification of CP and RP requires both to be deposited into PSGs.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 establish the conceptual framework based on prior work and current findings. Claims C99-C104 provide direct biochemical evidence through affinity purification and SDS-PAGE/immunoblotting showing that CP and RP co-purify in wild-type but not in Δblm10 or Δspg5 backgrounds during carbon starvation, supporting separate sequestration pathways.

results.result: RP-independent CP activity is unaltered by PSG formation, but RP-dependent CP activity is significantly reduced under carbon starvation, indicating CP-RP dissociation.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 provide proteasome activity assay data using two different substrates (Suc-LLVY-amc for CP alone, LFP for RP-dependent activity) showing differential effects of starvation conditions on CP versus RP-dependent activity. The data are consistent with prior work (C109) and support the dissociation model.

results.result: The deubiquitylase Ubp3 is specifically required for CP proteaphagy (but not RP proteaphagy) when PSG formation is blocked, requiring its catalytic activity and interaction with Bre5.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C120 provide confocal microscopy and GFP-release assay data in various double mutant backgrounds demonstrating Ubp3's selective effect on CP but not RP proteaphagy. Claims C121-C123 establish through complementation with wild-type and mutant variants that catalytic activity and Bre5 binding are required. Claims C124-C125 demonstrate specificity through systematic testing of other DUBs.

results.result: PSG formation promotes cell fitness and growth resumption after carbon starvation. Mutants unable to form PSGs show delayed growth recovery, which is partially suppressed by blocking autophagy or Ubp3. Pre-treatment with 2-DG or simultaneous carbon starvation improves recovery from nitrogen starvation.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C143 provide extensive growth resumption assays, amino acid analog sensitivity tests, and genetic epistasis experiments demonstrating that PSG formation improves cell fitness. The data include appropriate controls (C127-C128), complementation experiments (C137), and mechanistic insights through double mutant analyses (C138-C143), establishing a functional role for PSG-mediated proteasome protection.

results.result: Proteaphagy in Arabidopsis is selectively suppressed by fixed-carbon starvation (as in yeast), despite bulk autophagy being induced under all starvation conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C148 provide GFP-release assay data from Arabidopsis seedlings showing differential proteasome stability under nitrogen versus fixed-carbon starvation, with bulk autophagy measurements (C147) confirming that the effect is specific to proteaphagy. The parallel to yeast (C148) establishes evolutionary conservation.

results.result: Arabidopsis forms large cytoplasmic PSG-like structures upon fixed-carbon starvation that are distinct from autophagosomes and rapidly reversible.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C155 provide confocal microscopy data showing proteasome relocalization to vacuolar autophagic bodies under nitrogen starvation (C149) versus large cytoplasmic puncta under fixed-carbon starvation (C151). Claims C152-C153 establish through co-localization with ATG8a that these are not autophagosomes. Claims C154-C155 demonstrate rapid reversibility, paralleling yeast PSGs.

results.result: PA200 (the Arabidopsis ortholog of Blm10) is required for CP entry into PSGs and protection from proteaphagy in Arabidopsis, establishing evolutionary conservation of PSG function.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C161 provide GFP-release assays (C156-C157), confocal microscopy (C158-C159), and autophagy-independence experiments (C160-C161) demonstrating that PA200 functions analogously to yeast Blm10 in protecting the CP through PSG formation. Claim C162 synthesizes the evidence to establish evolutionary conservation across kingdoms.

results.result: PSGs represent an evolutionarily conserved mechanism that protects proteasomes from autophagic degradation during nutrient deprivation, promoting cell survival when growth conditions improve. Both CP and RP are sequestered separately via Blm10/PA200 and Spg5-dependent pathways.
results.evaluation: These claims represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing evidence from yeast (C1-C8) and Arabidopsis (C9) experiments. The claims are well-supported by the extensive experimental data throughout the manuscript, including genetic, biochemical, cell biological, and physiological approaches demonstrating the protective function of PSGs and their evolutionary conservation (C10, C163).

results.result: Protective aggregation similar to PSGs might occur for other protein complexes during stress, and proteasome dynamics could serve as a paradigm for studying biomolecular condensate formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C164-C165 are speculative proposals for future research directions based on the findings. While the speculation is reasonable given the results, no direct experimental evidence is provided for protective aggregation of other complexes or for using proteasomes as a general paradigm for condensate formation.
